title: 24 — Checklists, Runbooks & Interview Prep
html:
24 — Checklists, Runbooks & Interview Prep

The consolidated, printable layer. Everything here is a distillation of files 01–23 into things you use rather than read.

1. Design review checklist

Problem & scope

  • The problem is stated in one sentence, in business terms
  • Non-functional requirements have numbers (QPS, p99, availability, retention, cost)
  • Out-of-scope is explicit
  • The "do nothing / buy it / extend the existing thing" options were considered

Design

  • Context and container diagrams (C4 levels 1–2)
  • Data ownership unambiguous — exactly one writer per dataset
  • Consistency requirement stated per operation, and the UX for eventually-consistent paths is designed
  • Every external call has a timeout, a retry policy, and a defined failure behaviour
  • Idempotency where retries are possible
  • Scaling axis identified: which component scales, on which signal
  • Cache: layer, key, TTL, invalidation, cold-start capacity
  • The one-way-door decisions are named and have ADRs

Risk

  • Failure mode enumerated per dependency (slow / down / wrong data)
  • Blast radius bounded — bulkheads, rate limits, tenancy isolation
  • Graceful degradation ladder defined per feature
  • Migration and rollback path for the next two releases
  • Security: trust boundaries, authN/authZ, data classification, secrets
  • Cost at expected and 10× load

Operability

  • SLIs/SLOs defined; alerts planned
  • Correlation IDs, traces, structured logs, key metrics
  • Runbook for the top three predicted failures
  • Someone named owns it

2. Pull request checklist

As the author

  • The PR does one thing; the description says what and why (link the ticket/ADR)
  • Diff is under ~400 lines, or split
  • Tests: new logic covered; bug fixes have a regression test that fails without the fix
  • No commented-out code, no debug logging, no TODOs without a ticket
  • No secrets, no PII in logs, no hard-coded environment values
  • Errors handled explicitly; nothing swallowed; context preserved on rethrow
  • CancellationToken accepted and propagated on async paths
  • Public API changes are backward compatible, or versioned
  • Database changes are expand/contract-safe and reviewed as SQL
  • Observability added for new critical paths
  • I can explain every line in my own words

As the reviewer

  • Does it do what the ticket asks — no more, no less?
  • Edge cases: null/empty, zero, negative, max, concurrent, duplicate, timezone/DST, rounding
  • Is it in the right layer? (no business logic in controllers/components)
  • Any new abstraction justified by a real second use or a test seam?
  • Security: parameterised SQL, authZ server-side, input validated, output encoded
  • Performance: N+1, unbounded result sets, blocking calls, allocations in hot paths
  • Tests assert behaviour, not implementation
  • Names reveal intent; domain vocabulary used consistently
  • Separate blocking comments from nit: suggestions; explain the why and the cost

3. Production readiness checklist

Area Item
Health /health/live and /health/ready; readiness doesn't hard-fail on shared dependencies
Shutdown SIGTERM handled; drain window; shutdown timeout > longest request
Scaling Stateless verified at N>1 (sessions, caches, schedulers, websockets)
Resources Requests/limits from measured usage; memory limit set
Resilience Timeouts, jittered retries on idempotent ops only, circuit breakers, bulkheads
Data Backups configured and a restore tested; RPO/RTO written down
Security Secrets in a vault, least-privilege identity, TLS, headers, dependency scan clean
Observability Structured logs, RED metrics, traces, correlation, SLO dashboards and alerts
Runbook Top five alerts: symptom → diagnosis → mitigation → escalation
Rollback Proven, not theoretical; feature flags for risky changes
Load Tested at 2× peak; the failure mode past the ceiling is known
Cost Estimated, tagged, alerting on anomalies
Ownership On-call rota, escalation path, documented owner

4. Incident runbook (the generic one)

flowchart TD
    A[Alert or report] --> B["1. Assess: what is the USER impact?<br/>How many? Which regions/tenants?"]
    B --> C["2. Declare: severity + incident commander<br/>+ single comms channel"]
    C --> D["3. MITIGATE FIRST<br/>roll back · fail over · disable the feature ·<br/>shed load · scale out"]
    D --> E{Impact stopped?}
    E -->|No| F["Escalate; try the next mitigation.<br/>Diagnose only as far as needed to mitigate"]
    F --> D
    E -->|Yes| G["4. Diagnose properly:<br/>what changed → metrics → traces → logs"]
    G --> H["5. Fix forward + verify"]
    H --> I["6. Blameless postmortem within 5 days:<br/>timeline, contributing factors,<br/>detection and mitigation gaps,<br/>actions with owners and dates"]

The first four questions, in order:

  1. What changed? (deploys, config, flags, upstream, certificates, DNS, quota)
  2. What's the blast radius? (one user / one tenant / one region / everyone)
  3. Is it getting worse? (rate of change decides urgency)
  4. What's the fastest way to stop the pain? (not "what's the root cause")

Rules: mitigate before diagnosing; one person communicates; keep a timestamped timeline in the channel as you go; preserve evidence (dumps, logs, a snapshot) before restarting; don't make two changes at once; hand over explicitly if it runs long.

5. The 60-second triage commands

# Is the box healthy?
uptime; free -m; df -h; dmesg | tail -20

# Who's using CPU / memory / disk?
top -b -n1 | head -20; iostat -xz 1 3

# Is the network path OK?
ss -tanp | awk '{print $1}' | sort | uniq -c    # TIME_WAIT / CLOSE_WAIT counts
mtr --report --report-cycles 10 api.example.com

# Is the app healthy? (.NET)
dotnet-counters monitor -p <pid> System.Runtime Microsoft.AspNetCore.Hosting
dotnet-stack report -p <pid>          # what every thread is doing right now
dotnet-dump collect -p <pid>

# Kubernetes
kubectl get pods -o wide --sort-by=.status.startTime
kubectl describe pod <pod> | tail -30          # events: OOMKilled, probe failures, scheduling
kubectl logs <pod> --previous --tail=200
kubectl top pods --sort-by=memory

# Database (SQL Server)
SELECT session_id, blocking_session_id, wait_type, wait_time, status
FROM sys.dm_exec_requests WHERE blocking_session_id <> 0;

6. Rapid-fire Q&A by topic

Networking (file 01)

  • TCP vs UDP? Reliable ordered stream with congestion control vs fire-and-forget datagrams. UDP when stale data is worthless or you're building your own reliability.
  • What happens when you type a URL and press Enter? DNS (cache→resolver→root→TLD→authoritative) → TCP handshake → TLS handshake → HTTP request → LB/gateway → app → DB → response → parse → render. Name a failure mode at each step.
  • Why is HTTP/3 on UDP? To eliminate TCP head-of-line blocking and enable 0-RTT resumption and connection migration.
  • 502 vs 504? Bad upstream response vs upstream didn't answer in time.
  • Works in Postman, fails in the browser? CORS or cookie SameSite/Secure.

Data structures & algorithms (files 03–04)

  • Array vs linked list in practice? Array — cache locality beats asymptotics until n is large and mid-insertions are frequent.
  • When is a hash map O(n)? All keys collide — bad hash, adversarial input, or a broken GetHashCode.
  • Top-K from a billion-item stream? Size-K min-heap: O(n log K) time, O(K) space.
  • "Minimise the maximum"? Binary search on the answer.
  • Why B+ trees for indexes? Height = log base fan-out matches the page-based I/O cost model; linked leaves make range scans sequential.

Design (files 05–07)

  • SOLID, with the cost of violating each? Give the cost, not the definition.
  • Strategy vs State? Client chooses vs the object transitions itself.
  • Monolith or microservices? Modular monolith first; extract on evidenced pressure. A wrong boundary is far more expensive than a later extraction.
  • When is event sourcing wrong? Almost always, unless audit/temporal query is the product — schema evolution and GDPR costs are permanent.
  • How do you find service boundaries? Bounded contexts from event storming; validate that a typical change touches one context and data ownership is unambiguous.

System design (files 08–09)

  • First question in any design? Scale and consistency requirements, with numbers.
  • How do you scale reads? Cache → read replicas → denormalised read model → CDN. In that order.
  • How do you scale writes? Batch → async/queue → partition/shard → separate hot data.
  • Cache stampede? Per-key single-flight lock, jittered TTLs, stale-while-revalidate, probabilistic early expiry.
  • Exactly-once? Not as delivery. At-least-once + idempotent consumers = exactly-once effect.
  • Design a URL shortener / feed / chat / rate limiter? File 08 §8.

Databases (files 10–11)

  • Why did the query get slow overnight? Statistics/plan change (parameter sniffing), data growth crossing a threshold, an index dropped, or a blocking change upstream.
  • Isolation levels? Read Committed default; snapshot/MVCC so readers don't block writers; serializable for write-skew.
  • NOLOCK? Read uncommitted — can miss or duplicate rows. Not a tuning tool.
  • Delete 100M rows without downtime? Batched deletes with a delay, partition switch, or create-new-and-swap.
  • SQL vs NoSQL? By access pattern, consistency need, and data shape — never by scale folklore.

Concurrency (file 12)

  • Concurrency vs parallelism vs asynchrony? Structure vs simultaneous execution vs non-blocking waiting.
  • Thread-pool starvation? Blocked pool threads + slow injection → high latency, low CPU, growing queue.
  • Why does .Result deadlock? Captured synchronization context; the continuation needs the thread that's blocked waiting for it.
  • The GIL? One thread executes Python bytecode at a time; released during I/O and in native extensions.

Security (file 13)

  • AuthN vs authZ? 401 vs 403; both server-side; authZ on every access, not just at navigation.
  • Where to store a JWT in a browser? HttpOnly+Secure+SameSite cookie plus anti-forgery; localStorage means any XSS is account takeover.
  • Prevent SQL injection? Parameterised queries; allow-list anything that can't be parameterised.
  • Secret committed to git? Rotate first, then assess, then clean history.
  • Prompt injection defence? Architectural — never grant the model authority you wouldn't grant the content author.

Messaging & APIs (files 14–15)

  • Reliable publish + DB write? Transactional outbox or CDC. Never dual-write.
  • Ordering with scaled consumers? Partition by entity key; ordering is per key. Retries can still reorder — decide explicitly.
  • Make POST retry-safe? Client-supplied idempotency key stored with the original response.
  • Version an API? Additive-only within a version; URI path for majors; deprecation + sunset headers; monitor per-consumer usage before removal.

Stacks (files 16–18)

  • Explain the generational GC / how async works / LOH. File 16 §10.
  • OnPush and change detection / RxJS operator choice. File 17 §11.
  • Why is Polars faster than pandas? Rust + multithreading + Arrow + lazy optimiser with pushdown, no index semantics.

AI (files 19–21)

  • RAG vs fine-tuning? Knowledge vs behaviour.
  • Why is my RAG returning junk? Measure retrieval separately — usually chunking, no hybrid search, or no reranking.
  • How do you evaluate an LLM feature? A versioned golden set in CI measuring faithfulness, retrieval recall, format compliance, cost, and latency.
  • How do you review AI-generated code? Hallucinated APIs and packages, outdated idioms, swallowed errors, missing cancellation, concurrency subtleties, tests that assert the implementation.

Quality & operations (files 22–23)

  • Is 100% coverage a good goal? No — coverage measures execution, not verification. Use coverage delta plus mutation testing on critical modules.
  • Why not alert on CPU? Symptom, not cause. Alert on SLO burn rate.
  • Percentiles vs averages? Users experience the tail; nobody experiences the average.
  • First thing in an incident? What changed, then blast radius, then mitigate.

7. Behavioural / leadership answers (STAR, with the senior signal)

Prepare five stories you can tell in two minutes each, and be ready to go three levels deeper on any of them:

Story The signal the interviewer is listening for
A production incident you led Calm process, mitigate-before-diagnose, blameless follow-up, a systemic fix (not "we were more careful afterwards")
A design decision you got wrong Genuine self-assessment, what the early warning sign was, what you now check for
A disagreement with a colleague or a stakeholder Disagree-and-commit, arguing from evidence and trade-offs, changing your mind when shown data
Something you shipped that mattered Business outcome and measurement, not technology name-dropping
Something you deliberately did NOT build Scope judgement, cost awareness, saying no well — the rarest and strongest signal

Structure: Situation (20 s) → Task (10 s) → Action (60 s — what you did, first person) → Result (20 s, with a number) → Reflection (10 s, what you'd change).

Senior/staff-level markers to weave in naturally: you consider the option you rejected; you quantify; you talk about blast radius and reversibility; you mention what you taught or documented; you name the trade-off rather than claiming a free win.

8. A 90-day study plan

Weeks Focus Output
1–2 Files 01–02: networking, infrastructure Trace a request end-to-end in your own system; run the 60-second triage on a real box
3–4 Files 03–04: DS & algorithms 2 problems/day; re-solve each after 3 days; implement LRU, token bucket, consistent hashing from scratch
5–6 Files 05–07: OOP, patterns, architecture Refactor one real module; write two ADRs for decisions already made
7–8 File 08: HLD Work all eight case studies on a whiteboard, timed, without notes
9 File 09: LLD Four machine-coding problems in 60 minutes each, code that compiles
10–11 Files 10–12: databases, concurrency Tune three real slow queries; read the execution plans; find one concurrency bug in your codebase
12 Files 13–15: security, messaging, APIs Threat-model one feature; review one API against the checklist
13 Files 16–18: your stacks Profile one real endpoint; fix the top bottleneck; measure the delta
14 Files 19–21: AI Build a small RAG prototype with an eval set of 30 cases
15 Files 22–23: quality, observability Add SLOs + burn-rate alerts to one service; write its runbook
16 File 24 Mock interviews: 2 HLD, 2 LLD, 1 behavioural. Record yourself; watch it back

The rule that makes this work: produce an artifact every week — a diagram, a refactored module, a tuned query, an ADR, a runbook. Reading without producing decays within a month.

9. Self-assessment

Rate yourself 1–5 on each. Anything at 1–2 that's relevant to your role is your next study target.

Area Can you…
Networking Diagnose a latency problem from client to database without guessing
Infrastructure Explain what happens between kubectl apply and traffic being served
Data structures Pick a structure and justify it in one sentence with the trade-off
Algorithms Recognise the pattern in an unseen problem and state the complexity
OO design Name the cost of violating each SOLID principle with a real example
Patterns Refactor into a pattern when a third variation appears — and resist before then
Architecture Find bounded contexts and defend a monolith-vs-services decision with evidence
HLD Estimate scale, choose stores, and name the bottleneck order
LLD Produce compiling, extensible, thread-safe code in 60 minutes
Relational DB Read an execution plan and fix the query
NoSQL/caching Choose a store from access patterns and design invalidation
Concurrency Diagnose thread-pool starvation and explain why .Result deadlocks
Security Threat-model a feature and name the control for each STRIDE category
Messaging Design an idempotent consumer with an outbox and a DLQ strategy
API design Version, paginate, and make mutations retry-safe
.NET Explain the GC, find a memory leak, profile a hot path
Angular/TS Explain change detection and pick the right RxJS flattening operator
Python/data Build an idempotent, validated, partitioned pipeline
ML Spot leakage and choose a metric that matches the business goal
LLM Build and evaluate a RAG system, and defend it against prompt injection
AI-assisted dev Use it with a verification discipline you can articulate
Testing Design a suite that makes change safe rather than slow
Observability Walk the metrics → changes → traces → logs ladder

10. The short version — twenty principles

  1. Measure before you optimise. Intuition about performance is wrong most of the time.
  2. Boring technology by default. Novelty is a budget; spend it where it wins.
  3. Make the change easy, then make the easy change.
  4. Name the trade-off. A recommendation without a stated cost isn't engineering.
  5. The database is usually the bottleneck. Check it first.
  6. Everything remote fails. Timeout, retry (idempotent only), circuit-break, degrade.
  7. Idempotency is the foundation of distributed correctness.
  8. Bound everything: page sizes, queues, retries, concurrency, iterations, token budgets, memory.
  9. Deny by default — authorisation, CORS, network policy, feature exposure.
  10. Validate at the boundary; trust the interior.
  11. Immutable is easier than synchronised.
  12. One writer per dataset.
  13. Cache with a stated staleness window, and plan for a cold cache.
  14. Expand → migrate → contract. Every schema and API change, every time.
  15. If it isn't observable, it isn't operable. Correlation IDs are non-negotiable.
  16. Alert on symptoms, not causes. Every alert needs an owner and a runbook.
  17. A backup you haven't restored is a hypothesis.
  18. Delete code. The cheapest, safest, fastest code is the code that isn't there.
  19. Write it down. ADRs, runbooks, and README updates outlive every conversation.
  20. You own every line you commit — whoever or whatever typed it.

End of the knowledge base. Return to 00_INDEX_AND_HOW_TO_USE for the file map and learning paths.
